caption:
Why was Tesla's Wardenclyffe tower torn down?

In 1901 J. P. Morgan gave Tesla $150,000 for a wireless station on Long Island that could reach London and ships at sea. Morgan took 51% of the company and its patents.

Then Tesla read that Marconi was sending signals over the horizon. He decided to scale up — bigger transmitter, image and telephone transmission, wireless power — and asked for more money. Morgan refused.

Tesla built anyway: a 187-foot wood tower, a 55-ton cupola, a shaft 120 feet down with iron pipes driven 300 feet out from the bottom, so that "the whole of this globe can quiver". It never operated. In July 1903, the night Morgan refused in writing, newspapers reported the tower shooting flashes into the night sky. Nobody explained it.

His mortgage was held by the proprietor of the Waldorf-Astoria, where he lived and owed about $20,000. Foreclosure followed. On July 4, 1917 the Smiley Steel Company dynamited the tower. The first blast only tilted it; the job took until September. The scrap sold for $1,750.

A wartime rumour said the government ordered it down over German spies. It was false, but the mortgages were kept off the public record, so Tesla could not give the real reason.

Still unresolved: four 100-foot tunnels described as radiating from the tower's base. Drainage, access, or part of the ground connection — nobody knows.

Photographs of Wardenclyffe circa 1902 and 1904, the 1917 demolition attributed to the American Press Association, and Tesla's patent drawing. All public domain.

cards.headline: Tesla's tower was <y>dynamited for scrap</y>
cards.note: Shoreham, Long Island. It never became operational.
cards.source: Wardenclyffe, Long Island, circa 1902 · public domain
cards.alt: Wooden latticework tower with flat disc top rising behind a long brick building.,

cards.headline: This photograph was <y>a plea for money</y>
cards.note: Taken in 1904 so Tesla could go back to J. P. Morgan and ask for the funds to finish the tower. Morgan had already refused.
cards.alt: Sepia photo: domed skeletal tower at right, brick laboratory and chimney at left.

cards.headline: He wanted to make <y>the Earth itself</y> resonate
cards.note: Tesla doubted radio waves were the answer. He planned to inject current into the ground and return it through a charged upper layer of the atmosphere.
cards.alt: Patent drawing: tall coil and mast on a tripod frame with two ring conductors.

cards.headline: Below the tower, <y>a shaft 120 feet deep</y>
cards.note: Wood and steel lined, with a stairway inside. From the bottom Tesla pushed iron pipes out 300 feet — "to have a grip on the earth".
cards.alt: Detail: brick powerhouse with arched windows under the tower's wooden legs.

cards.headline: The first blast <y>only tilted it</y>
cards.note: The Smiley Steel Company began dynamiting on July 4, 1917. The tower was not fully down until September. Scrap value: $1,750.
cards.alt: Grainy press photo of the tower's timber frame leaning after being dynamited.

cards.headline: The tunnels underneath <y>have never been explained</y>
cards.note: Four 100-foot passages are described as running north, south, east and west from the shaft. Drainage, access, or part of the ground connection — the accounts disagree. How Tesla meant to combine ground conduction with his atmospheric idea is unknown.
cards.alt: Distant view of the unfinished tower and laboratory in an empty Long Island field.
